known_final_diagnosis: In our case, the clinical aspect was highly suggestive for PR. The patient presented all essential clinical features (oval erythematous-squamous lesions, with scaly aspect, with centrifugal progressive extension), all optional clinical features (supraclavicular heraldic plaque before the eruption; lesions with a linear pattern, located on the thorax, abdomen, and on the upper and lower limbs, less than 10% of them being located towards the extremities) and without any exclusive clinical features (without vesicular aspect, without the involvement of the soles, palms, and facial area, and with negative serology for syphilis).

report.source_text: On dermatological examination, an eruption in the right supraclavicular area consisting of an oval erythematous squamous plaque, well delimited, of 2.5/1.5 cm, covered with white, adherent scales (herald patch) was observed. Disseminated oval erythematous-papulosquamous lesions, well delimited, with regular contour, with diameters of about 0.5 to 1 cm, with linear pattern, associated with pruritus, and with a centrifugal progressive extension (Fig. 1) were observed. The eruption did not involve the soles, palms, and facial area.

report.source_text: Given the persistence and progressive nature of the lesion during the 3 weeks, with associated pruritus and with an inflammatory skin appearance, treatment was initiated with systemic corticosteroid therapy - hydrocortisone hemisuccinate 200 mg/day for 7 days, and loratadine 10 mg 2 times a day. Topical medication with dermatocorticosteroids and emollients were used with partial remission of the lesions after 7 days (Fig. 2). Two weeks after the admission into the Infectious Diseases Department, the patient was discharged with partial resolution of the skin lesions, without respiratory manifestations, and with a negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR from nasal and pharyngeal swabs.

clinician.trajectory_summary: 54-year-old Caucasian female presented with a 3-week history of pruritic erythematous-squamous lesions that began on the trunk and upper limbs and extended to lower limbs. The rash was preceded by 1 week of respiratory symptoms (nasal obstruction, dysphagia, dry cough, retrosternal pain) and occurred in the context of confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (RT-PCR positive). Clinical examination revealed a characteristic supraclavicular herald patch (2.5/1.5 cm oval erythematous-squamous plaque with white adherent scales) followed by disseminated oval erythematous-papulosquamous lesions (0.5-1 cm diameter) arranged in a linear pattern with centrifugal progressive extension, sparing palms, soles, and facial area. Syphilis serology and HIV antibodies were negative, excluding secondary syphilis and HIV-associated dermatosis. The patient was treated with systemic corticosteroids (hydrocortisone hemisuccinate 200 mg/day for 7 days), loratadine 10 mg twice daily, and topical dermatocorticosteroids with emollients, achieving partial remission of lesions within 7 days. Two weeks after admission, the patient was discharged with partial resolution of skin lesions, resolution of respiratory manifestations, and negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Negative syphilis serology (luetic serology negative per E005); clinical features of PR (herald patch, linear pattern, centrifugal spread) are characteristic of PR rather than secondary syphilis

Clinical morphology and distribution pattern are pathognomonic for pityriasis rosea (herald patch, oval lesions, linear arrangement, centrifugal spread, sparing of palms/soles/face) rather than typical COVID-19 exanthem

remaining_uncertainties: Histopathological confirmation was not performed; diagnosis is based entirely on clinical morphology and distribution
Exact timeline of complete lesion resolution beyond the 2-week discharge note is not documented
Potential temporal relationship between SARS-CoV-2 infection and PR onset (whether viral infection triggered PR or coincidental) is not explicitly discussed
